question: Which sentence uses a hyphen correctly? (1 mark)
options: She is a well known author.
explanation: 'Well-known' is a compound adjective that comes before the noun, so it needs a hyphen.

question: Which of these words is correctly hyphenated? (1 mark)
explanation: A hyphen is used after the prefix 're-' when the root word begins with 'e', to avoid confusion (re-enter, not reenter).

question: A hyphen and a dash are the same length and have the same purpose. (1 mark)
explanation: A hyphen (-) is short and joins words or parts of words together. A dash (--) is longer and separates parts of a sentence.

question: Add hyphens where needed in this sentence: My eight year old brother has a part time job delivering the well read local newspaper. (2 marks)
answer: My eight-year-old brother has a part-time job delivering the well-read local newspaper.
explanation: 'Eight-year-old' (compound adjective before noun), 'part-time' (compound adjective), and 'well-read' (compound adjective before noun) all need hyphens.

question: When do compound adjectives need a hyphen? (1 mark)
options: When they come before the noun they describe
When they come after the noun they describe
answer: When they come before the noun they describe
explanation: Compound adjectives are hyphenated before the noun (a well-known author) but usually not after it (the author is well known).

question: Rewrite this sentence adding the correct hyphens: She made a last minute decision to join the long distance race. (1 mark)
answer: She made a last-minute decision to join the long-distance race.
explanation: 'Last-minute' and 'long-distance' are compound adjectives before nouns, so they need hyphens.

question: Which number is written correctly with hyphens? (1 mark)
explanation: Compound numbers from twenty-one to ninety-nine are hyphenated when written as words.

question: Which word in this sentence should have a hyphen? The team scored a hat trick in the second half. (1 mark)
explanation: 'Hat-trick' is a compound noun that is conventionally hyphenated.

question: Why is a hyphen needed in 're-cover'? (1 mark)
options: To show it means 'to cover again' not 'to recover'
To make it easier to read
answer: To show it means 'to cover again' not 'to recover'
explanation: The hyphen distinguishes 're-cover' (cover again) from 'recover' (get better), preventing ambiguity.

question: The prefix 'co-' always needs a hyphen (e.g. co-operate). (1 mark)
explanation: Many words with 'co-' can be written with or without a hyphen (cooperate/co-operate). Usage varies, though hyphens are common when the root begins with 'o'.

question: Write a sentence that includes a compound adjective with a hyphen. (1 mark)
answer: Example: We watched a breath-taking sunset over the sea.
explanation: Accept any sentence with a correctly hyphenated compound adjective before a noun.

question: Which sentence uses hyphens correctly? (1 mark)
options: My sister-in-law is a full time teacher.
My sister in law is a full-time teacher.
My sister-in-law is a full-time teacher.
answer: My sister-in-law is a full-time teacher.
explanation: 'Sister-in-law' is a hyphenated compound noun. 'Full-time' is a compound adjective before the noun 'teacher'.

question: Rewrite this sentence with correct hyphens: There are thirty three well behaved children in the year six class. (1 mark)
answer: There are thirty-three well-behaved children in the year six class.
explanation: 'Thirty-three' (compound number) and 'well-behaved' (compound adjective before noun) need hyphens.

question: Which fraction is correctly hyphenated? (1 mark)
explanation: Fractions written as words are hyphenated (one-half, two-thirds, three-quarters).

question: Explain how a hyphen changes the meaning of these two phrases: 'a man eating chicken' and 'a man-eating chicken'. (2 marks)
answer: 'A man eating chicken' means a man who is eating some chicken. 'A man-eating chicken' means a chicken that eats men! The hyphen joins 'man' and 'eating' into a compound adjective describing the chicken.
explanation: Award 1 mark for explaining each phrase correctly, showing how the hyphen changes the meaning.

question: Find and correct the hyphen errors in this sentence: My ten year old cousin built a brightly-coloured, state of the art model aeroplane. (2 marks)
answer: My ten-year-old cousin built a brightly coloured, state-of-the-art model aeroplane.
explanation: 'Ten-year-old' needs hyphens (compound adjective). 'Brightly coloured' does not need a hyphen (adverb ending in -ly). 'State-of-the-art' needs hyphens (compound adjective before noun).

question: Which prefix usually requires a hyphen when added to a proper noun? (1 mark)
options: All of these when before a proper noun
answer: All of these when before a proper noun
explanation: A hyphen is used when a prefix is added to a proper noun (e.g. anti-European, pro-British, un-American).

question: Adverbs ending in '-ly' do not need a hyphen when forming a compound modifier (e.g. 'a quickly moving train' not 'a quickly-moving train'). (1 mark)
explanation: When the first word is an adverb ending in '-ly', no hyphen is needed because the '-ly' already signals that the word modifies the adjective.

question: Sort these into two groups - needs a hyphen and does not need a hyphen: twenty five, ice cream, self control, badly made, high quality fabric, deeply felt (2 marks)
answer: Needs a hyphen: twenty-five, self-control, high-quality fabric. Does not need a hyphen: ice cream, badly made, deeply felt.
explanation: Compound numbers, 'self-' compounds, and compound adjectives before nouns need hyphens. '-ly' adverb modifiers and established open compounds do not.
